lead: The engine takes chemical energy in with the fuel and turns part of it into work at the shaft. The rest leaves as heat, and it must go somewhere: into the cooling water, up the exhaust pipe, or out through the block by radiation and convection. A heat balance is a sheet that lists these streams in kW and as a percentage of the fuel power, and shows that they add up. It is how a test cell answers the question 'where did the fuel money go?', and it is how radiators and exhaust heat recovery equipment are sized.
prereq: You need: fuel power and brake thermal efficiency from the chapter on performance parameters, and brake power and fuel flow measurement from the chapter on fuel and air measurement.

sections.h3: The sheet, and why it must close

blocks.text: Chemical energy enters the engine at one rate and leaves at several. The rate at which the fuel brings energy in is the fuel power:

blocks.where: P<sub>f</sub> is the fuel power in kW, m<sub>f</sub> is the fuel mass flow in kg/h, CV is the calorific value of the fuel in MJ/kg, and 3.6 converts kg/h × MJ/kg into kW.

blocks.text: On the output side there are four streams: brake power P<sub>b</sub> at the shaft, heat to the cooling water P<sub>c</sub>, heat carried away by the exhaust gas P<sub>e</sub>, and the rest P<sub>u</sub>, which covers radiation, convection, heat to the lubricating oil (when an oil cooler is not measured separately) and any fuel that did not burn completely. Energy is conserved, so:
P<sub>f</sub> is fuel power, P<sub>b</sub> is brake power, P<sub>c</sub> is heat to cooling water, P<sub>e</sub> is heat in the exhaust gas, and P<sub>u</sub> is the unaccounted remainder, all in kW.
Only a few universities teach the heat balance as a full topic, but test cells draw one for every new engine. Each term is then also written as a percentage of P<sub>f</sub>.
Brake power comes from the dynamometer (see the chapter on measuring indicated, brake and friction power. The cooling water term comes from the water itself:
m<sub>w</sub> is the cooling water mass flow in kg/s, c<sub>pw</sub> is the specific heat of water, 4.18 kJ/kgK, and ΔT<sub>w</sub> is the rise in water temperature across the jacket in K.
The exhaust term is the sensible heat in the gas above ambient:
m<sub>g</sub> is the exhaust gas mass flow in kg/s, c<sub>pg</sub> is about 1.05 kJ/kgK for exhaust gas, and ΔT<sub>g</sub> is the exhaust temperature minus the ambient air temperature in K.

items: Water flow by rotameter, or by filling a bucket for a measured time; water temperatures by thermometers at the jacket inlet and outlet.
Exhaust gas flow is air flow plus fuel flow, mg = ma + mf, both measured as in the chapter on fuel and air measurement. Using air alone understates Pe.

An exhaust gas calorimeter checks the exhaust figure: the gas passes through a water-cooled heat exchanger, and the exhaust heat is the heat taken by the calorimeter water plus the heat still in the gas leaving it, P<sub>e</sub> = m<sub>wc</sub> × c<sub>pw</sub> × ΔT<sub>wc</sub> + m<sub>g</sub> × c<sub>pg</sub> × (T<sub>out</sub> − T<sub>room</sub>).
P<sub>u</sub> is not measured. It is P<sub>f</sub> minus the other three terms.

blocks.text: Two rules keep the sheet honest. First, every percentage is taken on P<sub>f</sub>, never on P<sub>b</sub>. Second, all four terms must be in the same unit before they are added; kW throughout is easiest, so a figure in kJ/h must be divided by 3600 first.

Draw the sheet as a bar or a divided block: one long bar of 100 % cut into four pieces, largest first. A pie chart with four thin slices is hard to read at a glance; a bar shows at once that brake power, cooling water and exhaust each take close to a third of the fuel energy in the worked example below.

The unaccounted term shrinks as the engine gets hotter. A cold engine stores heat in its metal and oil, and that stored heat lands in P<sub>u</sub>. Once the engine holds a steady temperature, the storage stops and P<sub>u</sub> falls to a small radiation and convection figure.

examples.question: An engine burns 3.0 kg/h of fuel of calorific value 42 MJ/kg and delivers 10.5 kW at the brake. It draws 90 kg/h of air. Cooling water flows at 8 kg/min and rises 18 °C across the jacket. The exhaust leaves 400 K above room temperature, with c<sub>pg</sub> = 1.05 kJ/(kg·K). Draw up the heat balance in kW and in percent.
steps: Fuel power: P<sub>f</sub> = m<sub>f</sub> × CV / 3.6 = 3.0 × 42 ÷ 3.6 = 35.0 kW.
Cooling water: m<sub>w</sub> = 8 ÷ 60 = 0.1333 kg/s, so P<sub>c</sub> = 0.1333 × 4.18 × 18 = 10.03 kW.
Exhaust gas flow: m<sub>g</sub> = m<sub>a</sub> + m<sub>f</sub> = 90 + 3.0 = 93 kg/h = 93 ÷ 3600 = 0.02583 kg/s. (The air-fuel ratio is 90 ÷ 3.0 = 30, a normal diesel value.)
Percentages of fuel power: brake 10.5 ÷ 35.0 = 30.0 %; cooling 10.03 ÷ 35.0 = 28.7 %; exhaust 10.85 ÷ 35.0 = 31.0 %; unaccounted 3.62 ÷ 35.0 = 10.3 %.
Check: 30.0 + 28.7 + 31.0 + 10.3 = 100.0 %, so the sheet closes on fuel power.
examples.answer: Fuel power 35.0 kW splits into 10.5 kW brake (30.0 %), 10.03 kW to cooling water (28.7 %), 10.85 kW in the exhaust (31.0 %) and 3.62 kW unaccounted (10.3 %).

traps: The sheet closes on fuel power, not on brake power. Percentages taken on the 10.5 kW of brake power would give 100 % for the brake and nonsense for the rest.
Exhaust mass flow is air plus fuel, m<sub>a</sub> + m<sub>f</sub>, not air alone; using air alone loses the fuel mass and understates the exhaust heat.
Never mix units on one sheet: kW, kJ/h and kcal/min must all be converted to a single unit before adding.
Use the temperature rise, not the absolute temperature: ΔT<sub>g</sub> is exhaust minus ambient, and ΔT<sub>w</sub> is outlet minus inlet. A rise of 18 K is the same as a rise of 18 °C.
Mass flows must be in kg/s before multiplying by c<sub>p</sub> × ΔT: divide kg/h by 3600 and kg/min by 60.

quiz.q: Name the four output terms of an engine heat balance.
quiz.a: Brake power, heat to cooling water, heat carried by the exhaust gas, and the unaccounted term (radiation, convection, oil cooler, incomplete combustion).

quiz.q: Which term of the heat balance is not measured, and how is it obtained?
quiz.a: The unaccounted term. It is fuel power minus brake power, cooling water heat and exhaust heat.

quiz.q: Why are the percentages of a heat balance taken on fuel power and not on brake power?
quiz.a: Fuel power is the total energy entering the engine, so every output is a fraction of that one input. Dividing by brake power would make the brake term 100 % and the fractions would no longer describe the fuel energy, and would not add to 100 %.

quiz.q: An engine uses 4.0 kg/h of fuel of calorific value 43 MJ/kg and gives 14 kW at the brake. Cooling water flows at 10 kg/min with an 18 °C rise; exhaust gas flows at 0.035 kg/s with c<sub>p</sub> = 1.05 kJ/(kg·K) and a 380 K rise. Find the unaccounted heat in kW and as a percentage of fuel power.
Convert a fuel flow of 3.0 kg/h and a cooling water flow of 8 kg/min into the units used in c<sub>p</sub> × ΔT formulas.
Why does the unaccounted term fall as the engine reaches steady hot condition?
quiz.a: A cold engine absorbs heat into its metal, oil and coolant bulk, and that stored heat appears in the remainder. At steady temperature no more heat is stored, so the remainder reduces to radiation, convection and small losses.

quiz.q: An exhaust gas calorimeter takes 0.08 kg/s of water, which rises 20 K. The exhaust gas, 0.025 kg/s with c<sub>pg</sub> = 1.05 kJ/(kg·K), leaves the calorimeter 60 K above room temperature. Find the heat carried by the exhaust.
quiz.a: Heat to calorimeter water = 0.08 × 4.18 × 20 = 6.69 kW. Heat still in the gas = 0.025 × 1.05 × 60 = 1.58 kW. Exhaust heat = 6.69 + 1.58 = 8.26 kW.

quiz.q: A student's heat balance comes out with a negative unaccounted term. Give three likely mistakes.
quiz.a: An exhaust mass flow larger than air plus fuel (or a flow in kg/h used as kg/s); the absolute exhaust temperature used instead of the rise above room temperature; terms in different units (kJ/min with kW) added together. Any of these inflates an output term above what the fuel supplied.

beyond: Not for the exam. Heat balances are the starting point for waste heat recovery: organic Rankine cycles, turbo-compounding and thermoelectric generators all feed on the exhaust term. The same sheet sizes radiators and decides fan power. Detailed balances split the remainder further, for example into the chemical energy of CO and unburnt fuel, measured with gas analysers. Search 'engine heat balance sheet', 'exhaust energy recovery Rankine cycle' and 'turbo compounding' to go further.
